precepts.text: He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant; the king made him lord of his house, to bind his princes at his pleasure and teach his senators wisdom.
precepts.point: The Most High called for the famine and sent a man before them, even Joseph: sold for a servant, his feet hurt with fetters, laid in iron until the time that his word came; then the king loosed him and made him lord of his house, to bind his princes at his pleasure and teach his senators wisdom. Whether prince or common man, Joseph could bind any man in Egypt.

note.label: Genesis 41: Pharaoh's Dreams and Joseph's Rise Over Egypt

precepts.why:
“Moreover he called for a famine upon the land: he brake the whole staff of bread. He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant.” The famine was the Most High’s doing, and so was the man sent ahead of it. Joseph was sold for a servant, his feet “they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron: Until the time that his word came: the word of the Lord tried him.”

Then the turn: “The king sent and loosed him; even the ruler of the people, and let him go free. He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance: To bind his princes at his pleasure; and teach his senators wisdom.” That is Pharaoh setting Joseph over his house and over all the land of Egypt, with the ring, the fine linen, the gold chain and the second chariot, and “only in the throne will I be greater than thou.”

To bind his princes at his pleasure: whether prince or common man, Joseph could bind any man in Egypt. “without thee shall no man lift up his hand or foot in all the land of Egypt”; nothing moved unless Joseph decreed it.

precepts.text: Touch not mine anointed; he called for a famine and sent a man before them, even Joseph, whose feet they hurt with fetters.
precepts.point: The famine itself was called by the Most High, and the man was sent before them, even Joseph, sold for a servant, whose feet they hurt with fetters. The fetters and the iron are the prison where the king's prisoners were bound.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“Saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm. Moreover he called for a famine upon the land: he brake the whole staff of bread. He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant: Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron.”

The famine itself was called by the Most High, and the man was sent before them, even Joseph. That is why Joseph could say “God did send me before you to preserve life”, and “it was not you that sent me hither, but God.” The selling for a servant, the fetters and the iron were all the road the Lord sent him down ahead of the famine to save his brethren’s lives by a great deliverance.

precepts.text: The word of the Lord tried him; the king loosed him and made him lord of his house, to teach his senators wisdom; then Israel also came into Egypt.
precepts.point: Jacob knew there was corn in Egypt because Joseph had already told Pharaoh exactly what to do to save up in the time of tribulation; when Jacob heard, he sent out the fathers. Applying these attributes makes better men, women, brothers, and sisters, to bring forth the nation unto the kingdom of God.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“Until the time that his word came: the word of the Lord tried him.” Joseph sat in the prison until the time that his word came; the word of the Lord tried him. Then “The king sent and loosed him; even the ruler of the people, and let him go free. He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance: To bind his princes at his pleasure; and teach his senators wisdom.”

That is who the brethren told Jacob about: “Joseph is yet alive, and he is governor over all the land of Egypt.” He was the teacher in Egypt, teaching Pharaoh’s senators wisdom, second in command, a king in all but title. Everything Egypt was at that point in time came through the influence of Joseph; the prosperity of that land was the favor the Lord had with Israel.

Then “Israel also came into Egypt; and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham. And he increased his people greatly; and made them stronger than their enemies.” That is Jacob’s answer here, “I will go and see him before I die”, and what came of it.

precepts.text: Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm; Pharaoh's threat against Moses could not stand.
precepts.point: The Egyptians were urgent upon the people to send them out of the land in haste, for they said, We be all dead men.

note.label: Exodus 12: The Lord's Passover

precepts.why:
The last time Pharaoh saw Moses he threatened to kill him if he ever saw his face again. Now he “called for Moses and Aaron by night, and said, Rise up, and get you forth from among my people, both ye and the children of Israel; and go, serve the Lord, as ye have said. Also take your flocks and your herds, as ye have said, and be gone; and bless me also.”

“Saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.” Pharaoh's threat against Moses could not stand, because Moses was the Lord's anointed and his prophet. The man who thought he could threaten the servant of the Most High had a complete change of tone: from a threat of death to “bless me also.” There was not a house in Egypt where there was not one dead, and the Egyptians were urgent to send Israel out, saying, “We be all dead men.” The Lord's prophet was not touched; Egypt was.

precepts.text: The same everlasting covenant to a thousand generations, made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
precepts.point: The covenant was made with Abraham, sworn to Isaac, and confirmed to Jacob as an everlasting covenant, giving Israel the land of Canaan as their inheritance.

note.label: 1 Chronicles 16: The Song Delivered into the Hand of Asaph

precepts.why:
“He hath remembered his covenant for ever, the word which he commanded to a thousand generations. Which covenant he made with Abraham, and his oath unto Isaac; And confirmed the same unto Jacob for a law, and to Israel for an everlasting covenant”. It is the same song and the same everlasting covenant.

The Most High is mindful always of his covenant, and a thousand generations is to say forever. It was made with Abraham, sworn to Isaac and confirmed to Jacob as an everlasting covenant, “Saying, Unto thee will I give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance”.

precepts.text: Whatever was written before was written for our learning, that we might have hope.
precepts.point: Remember His marvelous works, His wonders, and the judgments of His mouth. The Bible tells us to remember our past.

note.label: Psalm 105: Remember His Marvelous Works from Abraham to the Exodus

precepts.why:
“Remember his marvellous works that he hath done; his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth”. The Bible tells us to remember our past, and Paul gives the reason it was written down: “whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.”

The works of the Most High for our fathers were not recorded for a history lesson. They were written so that we, reading them now, might learn and have hope. That is why the psalm calls us to make known his deeds among the people, to talk of all his wondrous works and to seek his face evermore.

precepts.text: Stand in the ways and ask for the old paths and walk therein; but they said we will not.
precepts.point: Remember His marvelous works, His wonders, and the judgments of His mouth. The Bible tells us to remember our past.

note.label: Psalm 105: Remember His Marvelous Works from Abraham to the Exodus

precepts.why:
“Thus saith the Lord, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls.” Remembering his marvellous works and the judgments of his mouth is asking for the old paths, the good way our fathers walked, and the rest for our souls is found in walking in it.

“But they said, We will not walk therein.” Israel refused. The psalm calls us the other way: give thanks unto the Lord, call upon his name, glory in his holy name and remember what he has done, so that we do not answer as they did.

precepts.text: The Most High was with Joseph and made him overseer over the house of his Egyptian master.
precepts.point: The king loosed him and made him lord of his house and ruler of his substance, to bind his princes and teach his senators wisdom. Our forefather Joseph taught the Egyptians; those who boast in Egyptology forget our forefathers taught them.

note.label: Psalm 105: Remember His Marvelous Works from Abraham to the Exodus

precepts.why:
“He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant”. Genesis shows the Most High with him in that servitude: “the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian.”

“And his master saw that the Lord was with him, and that the Lord made all that he did to prosper in his hand. And Joseph found grace in his sight, and he served him: and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.” The Egyptian master himself saw that the Lord was with Joseph and put everything he had into his hand.

This is the beginning of what the psalm ends with: the king loosed him and “made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance”, to bind his princes at his pleasure “and teach his senators wisdom.” Our forefather Joseph taught the Egyptians. Those who boast in Egyptology forget that our forefathers taught them.

precepts.text: The Egyptians dealt subtly with Israel and turned to hate them.
precepts.point: He smote all the firstborn, the chief of all their strength. The firstborn is the chief of one's strength, as Reuben was Jacob's strength before he lost it.

note.label: Psalm 105: Remember His Marvelous Works from Abraham to the Exodus

precepts.why:
“He turned their heart to hate his people, to deal subtilly with his servants.” Exodus shows how: “there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph”, and he said, “Behold, the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we: Come on, let us deal wisely with them; lest they multiply”.

That is the Most High increasing his people greatly and making them stronger than their enemies, just as the psalm says, and the Egyptians fearing it. “Therefore they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens. And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses. But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew.”

“And the Egyptians made the children of Israel to serve with rigour: And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field”. Israel came into Egypt and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham, and the Egyptians dealt subtilly with Israel and turned to hate them. Then he sent Moses his servant and Aaron whom he had chosen, with his signs and wonders in the land of Ham.

precepts.text: Tithes are meat for the storehouse, not money; when the nation is righteous He rebukes the devourer so it destroys not the fruit of the ground.
precepts.point: He smote all the firstborn, the chief of all their strength. The firstborn is the chief of one's strength, as Reuben was Jacob's strength before he lost it.

note.label: Psalm 105: Remember His Marvelous Works from Abraham to the Exodus

precepts.why:
“He spake, and the locusts came, and caterpillers, and that without number, And did eat up all the herbs in their land, and devoured the fruit of their ground.” That is the devourer, and in Malachi the Most High promises to rebuke it for the sake of a righteous nation: “I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground; neither shall your vine cast her fruit before the time in the field”.

“Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings. Ye are cursed with a curse: for ye have robbed me, even this whole nation.” The tithe is “meat in mine house”: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house”. Tithes are meat for the storehouse, not money.

What fell on Egypt as a plague is what the Most High holds back from a righteous nation. When the nation is righteous he rebukes the devourer so that it does not destroy the fruit of the ground; he opens the windows of heaven and pours out a blessing “that there shall not be room enough to receive it.”

precepts.text: Coupled with Malachi, the tithe was tied to the Levitical priesthood; our duty now is alms.
precepts.point: He smote all the firstborn, the chief of all their strength. The firstborn is the chief of one's strength, as Reuben was Jacob's strength before he lost it.

note.label: Psalm 105: Remember His Marvelous Works from Abraham to the Exodus

precepts.why:
“Thou shalt truly tithe all the increase of thy seed, that the field bringeth forth year by year.” The tithe was of the increase of the seed, what the field brought forth, which is why Malachi calls it meat for the storehouse.

Coupled with Malachi, the tithe was tied to the Levitical priesthood. Our duty now is alms.

precepts.text: Disobedience brings the diseases of Egypt to cleave unto us, such as we suffer today.
precepts.point: He gave them the lands of the heathen and the labor of the people, that they might keep His statutes and laws. But we were not thankful, we went into idolatry, and now we are scattered in Babylon in America.

note.label: Psalm 105: Remember His Marvelous Works from Abraham to the Exodus

precepts.why:
“He brought them forth also with silver and gold: and there was not one feeble person among their tribes.” Not one feeble person coming out of Egypt. Look at the sicknesses we suffer now under the curses.

Deuteronomy tells why: “If thou wilt not observe to do all the words of this law that are written in this book, that thou mayest fear this glorious and fearful name, THE LORD THY GOD; Then the Lord will make thy plagues wonderful, and the plagues of thy seed, even great plagues, and of long continuance, and sore sicknesses, and of long continuance.”

“Moreover he will bring upon thee all the diseases of Egypt, which thou wast afraid of; and they shall cleave unto thee.” The very diseases of Egypt that Israel walked out from, whole and strong, come back and cleave to us through disobedience. That is the sickness we suffer today.

precepts.text: Because we served not the Most High with joyfulness for the good given us, these curses came; remember why we are here.
precepts.point: He gave them the lands of the heathen and the labor of the people, that they might keep His statutes and laws. But we were not thankful, we went into idolatry, and now we are scattered in Babylon in America.

note.label: Psalm 105: Remember His Marvelous Works from Abraham to the Exodus

precepts.why:
He gave them the lands of the heathen and the labour of the people, “That they might observe his statutes, and keep his laws.” Everything he did, the cloud for a covering, the fire for light, the quails, the bread of heaven and the water out of the rock, was done so that Israel would keep his laws.

But we were not thankful. “Because thou servedst not the Lord thy God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, for the abundance of all things”: that is why the curses came. We went into idolatry, and now we are scattered in Babylon in America.

Remember why we are here. He remembered his holy promise to Abraham and brought forth his people with joy; we did not serve him with joyfulness for the good given us.
